forces: Piano, flute, oboes, bassoons, horns and strings
performers: Artur Schnabel, piano; London Symphony Orchestra, Malcolm Sargent
intro: In this F major Andante from the Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major, K. 467, muted violins play the melody over repeated triplets and a plucked bass. Artur Schnabel takes up the melody, which later returns in A♭ before coming back to F major.

sections.label: A · Muted violins, pizzicato bass
sections.mNote: Inner strings repeat triplets beneath the long melody.

sections.label: A′ · Piano takes the melody
sections.mNote: Left-hand triplets accompany the right-hand melody.

sections.label: B · Winds alternate with the piano
sections.mNote: The orchestra plays between the piano’s solo phrases.

sections.label: A″ · The tune returns in A♭
sections.mNote: Piano and plucked strings play the opening phrase again.

sections.label: Coda · Back towards F major
sections.mNote: Piano ornaments over held winds lead to the final cadence.

cues.title: Opening, muted strings and pizzicato bass
cues.text: Second violins and violas repeat soft triplets above plucked cellos and basses. The muted first violins enter with the melody in long phrases over this accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, opening, p. 31: muted strings, triplet accompaniment and pizzicato bass. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/9/95/IMSLP442212-PMLP05554-mozartpianoconcertoNo.21score.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violin melody, leaps and dissonances
cues.text: The violin melody rises into wide leaps and accented dissonances, and the winds support the clashes. The dynamic stays soft. The triplet accompaniment continues beneath the changing chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, opening orchestral statement, pp. 31–32. The dissonances and leaps are discussed by Hannah Chan-Hartley: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36107.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Solo entry, piano
cues.text: At the solo entry the piano’s left hand takes over the repeated triplets and the right hand plays the melody. All the strings play pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, bars 23–26, p. 32.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The film Elvira Madigan, 1967
cues.text: The Swedish film Elvira Madigan (1967) used this Andante, in a recording by Géza Anda, and the concerto took its nickname from the film. Schnabel’s performance, heard here, was made thirty years earlier.
cues.evidence: Roy Hemming, Discovering Music (1974), and Joel Whitburn, Top Pop Albums 1955–1992 (1993): Géza Anda’s Mozart Concertos 17 and 21 on Deutsche Grammophon were the film’s sound track and were sold in the United States as “Elvira Madigan” (full-text excerpts seen, pages not recorded; the film’s 1967 date not checked against a primary record). Schnabel’s session date: https://archive.org/details/Mozart.PianoConcertoNo.21

cues.title: Recording, Abbey Road, 1937
cues.text: Schnabel recorded this concerto on a Bechstein in Abbey Road’s Studio 1 on 12 January 1937, with Malcolm Sargent conducting the London Symphony Orchestra. The Andante took up two sides of the original HMV issue.
cues.evidence: John Bolig, HMV discography, K. 467 entries: Schnabel’s Bechstein, the players, session and Andante matrices 2EA4608–4609 on DB3101. https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Bolig2020.pdf#page=530.

cues.title: Middle section, winds and strings
cues.text: Winds and strings alternate with the piano, then the soloist resumes above the repeated accompaniment. The orchestral phrases become sharper as the middle passage goes on.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, bars 55–69, pp. 35–36.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening melody, A♭ major
cues.text: After a brief break in the repeated accompaniment, the piano plays the opening melody again in A♭ major, a key far from F. Plucked strings and left-hand triplets return beneath it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, bars 70–77, pp. 36–37. Chan-Hartley explicitly identifies the A♭ major reprise.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: LP reissue, COLH 67, 1959
cues.text: This stream is Bob Varney’s transfer of the Angel LP COLH 67, issued in the series “Great Recordings of the Century”. The London Symphony Orchestra’s discography dates that reissue to November 1959, twenty-two years after the Abbey Road session.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive description of the transfer (Angel reissue mono LP COLH 67, transfer by Bob Varney): https://archive.org/details/Mozart.PianoConcertoNo.21 LSO discography, session 0158: COLH 67, November 1959: https://londonso-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2024/08/Discography-August-2024.pdf#page=289

cues.title: Return to F major
cues.text: The piano’s embellished line modulates back towards F major, with sustained woodwind notes beside it. The triplets continue through the final phrases and stop at the last cadence.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, closing pages 37–39; Chan-Hartley describes the modulations back to F major.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Triplets pass to the piano
transitions.how: The orchestra ends its opening statement in F major. The piano’s left hand takes up the triplets, and all the strings play pizzicato. The right-hand melody enters above this accompaniment, still in F major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, bars 22–26, p. 32.

transitions.title: Winds and strings during the piano’s rest
transitions.to: B · Winds alternate with the piano
transitions.how: The solo passage reaches C major. Winds and strings play while the piano rests, then the piano resumes with triplets beneath a held right-hand note. The pizzicato bass continues throughout.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, bars 55–61, p. 35.

transitions.title: Link to the melody in A♭ major
transitions.from: B · Winds alternate with the piano
transitions.to: A″ · The tune returns in A♭
transitions.how: The repeated accompaniment stops for a short time. Over held notes in the strings, the piano plays a connecting phrase, and the opening melody then returns in A♭ major. Under the tune the left hand takes up its triplets again and the strings go back to pizzicato.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, bars 68–76, pp. 36–37; Hannah Chan-Hartley, National Arts Centre programme note.

transitions.title: The return from A♭ to F major
transitions.from: A″ · The tune returns in A♭
transitions.how: The returning melody modulates out of A♭ by further steps towards F major. Piano triplets continue the accompaniment, and the winds hold notes under the soloist’s ornaments. The closing phrases return to F, and the repeated triplet motion stops.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, II, pp. 37–39; Chan-Hartley describes the return from A♭ to F.

source.title: Mozart, K. 467, full score: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1878; Broude reprint, plate 422
source.locator: II. Andante, printed pp. 31–39. Mozart leaves out trumpets and timpani for this movement.

timeline.note: Muted second violins and violas repeat triplets above plucked cellos and basses.
Muted first violins play the melody above the triplets and pizzicato bass.
Woodwinds and horns join the accented chords and answer the violins.
The piano plays both the melody and the triplets, accompanied by pizzicato strings.
Bowed violin phrases answer the piano above the continuing plucked bass.
Flute, oboes and bassoons answer with the strings before the piano resumes.
Piano phrases alternate with held wind chords above the strings’ accompaniment.
The piano restores the melody in A♭ over plucked strings; oboes and bassoons sustain its continuation.
Piano ornaments, held winds and repeating strings lead back to the F major cadence.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Artur Schnabel (piano), London Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Malcolm Sargent (conductor)
fields.note: The item description, source LP sleeve and LSO discography agree. The later sleeve’s title Sir is not used to infer Sargent’s title at the 1937 session.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any local editorial changes are not identified. The consulted full score establishes the movement’s original forces, including the absence of trumpets and timpani, but is not claimed to be the copy used at the session. The Archive description explicitly says that an earlier file mix-up with K. 595 has been corrected; the current attribution follows the corrected record. No bar-by-bar or aural authentication of the transfer has been made.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: LSO session 0158 dates K. 467 to 12 January 1937; the 9 January date in the same entry belongs to K. 459. Both Andante sides are dated 12 January in the side-level discographies.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The item names Abbey Road Studios; the LSO register, Bolig and Schnabel chronology specify Studio 1.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Angel Records — Great Recordings of the Century
fields.note: The Archive expressly identifies a mono LP transfer. Angel is the transferred reissue label; the original shellac issue was on His Master’s Voice.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: COLH 67 is visible on the photographed sleeve, which pairs K. 467 under Sargent with K. 595 under Barbirolli. The LSO discography dates the LP to November 1959 and the original K. 467 set, HMV DB3099–3102, to November 1937. The Andante occupied DB3101.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Probable original-side lineage: 2EA 4608-1 and 2EA 4609-2A; Andante parts 1–2 on HMV DB3101, concerto sides 5–6.
fields.note: The original issued matrices and takes are documented in both discographies, but their identity within this particular LP transfer has not been established by runout inspection or take comparison. The LP’s own matrix/runout and pressing are unknown. No side-join timing is assigned. A targeted DAHR search did not yield a usable session record, so no DAHR matrix entry is claimed.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The explicit source credit is ‘Transfer by Bob Varney’; it is not an assumption based on the uploader’s identity.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: 19 April 2010 is the item’s added date, not an identified transfer date. The later current-file timestamp and the correction notice likewise do not establish when the LP was digitised.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No cartridge, equalisation, restoration, editing or speed-correction procedure is documented. Internet Archive describes the file as original-upload VBR MP3; that descriptor does not imply access to an original recording master.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mozart’s concerto is public domain under the ordinary life-plus-70 authorship term.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791. The consulted public-domain full score derives from Breitkopf’s 1878 edition. This term calculation concerns the underlying composition and does not establish rights in an unidentified modern performing edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102.
fields.note: Publication before 1963 is documented by the orchestra’s discography, not inferred only from the session date. The ordinary EU 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. This is a territorial basis, not worldwide clearance. US public-domain status is not established; the recording was not first published by 1925. The uploader’s http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/ declaration does not independently establish authority to clear the original performers’ or producer’s rights in the US or elsewhere. The legal link below identifies the term basis rather than a Creative Commons licence.

dossier.credit: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major, K. 467, II. Andante. Artur Schnabel, piano; London Symphony Orchestra; Malcolm Sargent. Recorded 12 January 1937, Abbey Road Studio 1, London. Transfer by Bob Varney from Angel COLH 67, via Internet Archive. EU territorial public-domain basis; US status not established.

composer.epithet: Composer of operas in which a servant outwits a count, and of piano concertos in which the soloist sometimes enters before the orchestra has finished its opening.
facts: He usually called himself Wolfgang Amadè Mozart
Childhood tours across Europe; three Italian visits, 1769–73
His home from 1781; concertos, quartets and the Da Ponte operas
K. or KV: Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and revised since

quote.text: In an opera, poetry must simply be music’s obedient daughter.
quote.source: Mozart to his father Leopold, Vienna, 13 October 1781; our translation

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
